title: Why do people share ideologically extreme, false, and misleading content on social media? A self-report and trace data-based analysis of countermedia content dissemination on facebook and twitter
screen_reason: Trace-data study of US Qualtrics panellists whose Facebook and Twitter post histories were matched against a 106-domain 'countermedia' (fake news) list. Reports the share of respondents who shared at least one countermedia item on each platform (SHARING actor_share, derivable per R8 from verbatim counts) and, in a follow-up analysis, the share of all countermedia shares attributable to ideologically extreme users alongside that group's share of the sample (CONCENTRATION-type figures, flagged borderline because the group is defined by ideology, not by activity rank).

estimates.date: posts coded 1 August 2015 to 6 June 2017; survey and data harvest 7 March to 6 June 2017
estimates.measure_type: % of surveyed Facebook users who shared at least one countermedia (fake news domain) link on Facebook in the study window
estimates.value_raw: 196/678 users with non-zero countermedia share counts; 'The majority of respondents (71.1%) did not share any countermedia items'
estimates.denominator: 678 U.S. adults in the Facebook analytic sample (Qualtrics panel, active users of both Facebook and Twitter, >=50 posts on each)
estimates.definition: user posted at least one Facebook item containing a link to one of the 106 identified countermedia domains between 1 August 2015 and 6 June 2017
estimates.misinfo_def: countermedia content, or web-based, ideologically extreme information that uses false, biased, misleading, and hyper-partisan claims to counter the knowledge produced by the mainstream news media
estimates.source_quote: The majority of respondents (71.1%) did not share any countermedia items.
estimates.page_loc: Measures, Countermedia content sharing (p. 11); Modeling approach (p. 13); Note 6
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain list pooled from 11 published fake-news lists (About.com, Aloisius, CBS News, The Daily Dot, Fake News Watch, Fake News Checker, Melissa Zimdars, NPR, Snopes Field Guide, The New Republic, U.S. News and World Report); a site had to appear on at least two lists; authors manually removed parody sites and non-political sites; 106 domains retained, 62 actually shared. No intercoder reliability reported (list matching by Python script).
estimates.moderator_quote: To develop a comprehensive list of countermedia sites, we first generated a corpus of domains by pooling lists of so-called fake news domains published by About.com, Aloisius, CBS News, The Daily Dot, Fake News Watch, Fake News Checker, Melissa Zimdars, NPR, Snopes Field Guide, The New Republic, and U.S. News and World Report. ... To appear in our list, a site had to appear on at least two of the identified fake news domain lists. In total, we identified 106 countermedia websites.
estimates.notes: Value derived per R8 as an exact part/whole share from two verbatim counts with the same denominator (196 non-zero sharers / 678 analytic sample = 28.9%); it is the exact complement of the verbatim 71.1% who shared none, and Note 6 confirms the descriptives use the n = 678 analytic sample. Sharing window is ~22 months of exhaustive post history, so the figure is not comparable to short-window survey recall items. Source quote replaced (it was a three-part ellipsis join) with the single contiguous sentence it rests on. The value is not the complement 100-71.1, which R8 forbids, but the exact part/whole share from the paper's own counts: 196 Facebook respondents with a non-zero countermedia share count out of the analytic sample of 678 = 28.9%. Those counts are stated in two other contiguous spans: "for both the countermedia (n = 196) and mainstream news (n = 512) variables" and "(Facebook, n = 678; Twitter, n = 543)."

estimates.value_raw: 27/543 users with non-zero countermedia share counts; 'A large majority (95.0%) of respondents did not share any countermedia content'

estimates.misinfo_def: countermedia content, or web-based, ideologically extreme information that uses false, biased, misleading, and hyper-partisan claims to counter the knowledge produced by the mainstream news media
estimates.source_quote: A large majority (95.0%) of respondents did not share any countermedia content.
estimates.page_loc: Measures, Countermedia content sharing (p. 11); Modeling approach (p. 13)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 106-domain pooled fake-news list as the Facebook row; site had to appear on at least two of eleven published lists; parody and non-political sites removed by hand.
estimates.moderator_quote: A Python script was used to extract all social media posts that contained articles from the countermedia identified domains. Content from a total of 62 domains was shared across both platforms

Same respondents as the Facebook row for 525 of the cases, so the two platform rows are not independent samples. Source quote replaced (it was an ellipsis join) with the single contiguous sentence it rests on. As for the Facebook row, the value is the part/whole share from the paper's counts (27 Twitter respondents with non-zero countermedia sharing out of an analytic sample of 543 = 5.0%), not a computed complement of 95.0.

estimates.measure_type: % of all countermedia shares on Facebook accounted for by the 22.9% of the sample at the extreme ends of the ideology scale
estimates.value_raw: 43.4% of all countermedia shares from 22.9% of the analytic sample
estimates.conc_group_label: respondents at the extreme ends of the ideological spectrum (conservatism score of 1 or 7)
estimates.denominator: 1,152 countermedia content shares by 678 Facebook analytic-sample users
estimates.definition: share of all observed countermedia link shares posted by users scoring at either pole of the 7-point conservatism scale
estimates.misinfo_def: countermedia content, or web-based, ideologically extreme information that uses false, biased, misleading, and hyper-partisan claims to counter the knowledge produced by the mainstream news media
estimates.source_quote: In the Facebook sample, those scoring at the extreme ends of the ideological spectrum shared 43.4% of all countermedia shares, despite the fact that these categories only represented 22.9% of the analytic sample.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 106-domain pooled fake-news list; group membership from the self-reported 7-point conservatism scale rounded to the nearest whole number.
estimates.moderator_quote: To further explore this potential discrepancy with extant literature, we rounded the conservatism measure to the nearest whole number and examined the summed number of countermedia content shares across the scale range.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL: the group is defined by ideological extremity, not by sharing volume, so this is not a top-X%-of-sharers concentration statistic and will understate activity-ranked concentration. Both R1-required fields are nonetheless stated verbatim in one sentence. An adjudicator may prefer to drop it from any pooled concentration curve or keep it as an attitude-partition variant.

estimates.value_raw: 22.8% of the sample was responsible for 48.4% of all countermedia shares
estimates.conc_group_label: respondents at the extreme ends of the ideological spectrum (conservatism score of 1 or 7)
estimates.denominator: 128 countermedia content shares by 543 Twitter analytic-sample users
estimates.definition: share of all observed countermedia link shares posted by users scoring at either pole of the 7-point conservatism scale
estimates.misinfo_def: countermedia content, or web-based, ideologically extreme information that uses false, biased, misleading, and hyper-partisan claims to counter the knowledge produced by the mainstream news media
estimates.source_quote: On Twitter, this pattern was nearly identical: 22.8% of the sample was responsible for 48.4% of all countermedia shares.

estimates.moderator_quote: In the Twitter sample, those scoring a 7 on the conservatism measure accounted for 32.0% of all countermedia shares, again accounting for the highest per-category share percentage.
estimates.notes: Same judgement call as the Facebook concentration row: an ideology-defined partition, not an activity-ranked top-X%. The base is only 128 shares, and 27 sharers, so the estimate is unstable. quote_verbatim=false: the quote is the paper's sentence exactly, but the text rendering runs two words together ("was responsiblefor 48.4%"), so it is not byte-identical to the file.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Mean sharing intensities were not extracted as rows: Facebook overall mean 1.70 countermedia shares per user (SD = 8.54), 5.88 among sharers (SD = 15.11); Twitter 0.24 overall (SD = 1.94), 4.74 among sharers (SD = 7.49). These are per-capita counts over a ~22-month exhaustive post window and are not shares of anything; R4 favours the two clean actor_share rows. (2) No % of shared links that were countermedia is derivable: 1,152 countermedia and 7,468 mainstream news shares are given for Facebook (128 and 4,229 for Twitter), but the total number of links shared is never reported, so there is no denominator for a SHARING content_share row. (3) 'those scoring a 7 on the conservatism scale accounted for 25.6% of all countermedia shares' (Facebook) and 32.0% (Twitter) fail R1: no matching conc_group_pct is given for that single scale point. (4) 'Within this subsample, the five most active users shared over 75% of all shared content' is a genuine top-user concentration figure but refers to MAINSTREAM news sharing on Twitter, not misinformation, and is a bound ('over 75%'), so it was not extracted. (5) Mourao and Robertson's ~55% partisan-article figure cited in the literature review belongs to another paper (R8 bars figures cited from elsewhere).

rob.design: Qualtrics-recruited U.S. online panel (783 valid responses; 13.5% of those who engaged with the materials met inclusion criteria and gave valid responses, so no conventional response rate), quotas of ~50/50 sex, aged 18+, U.S. citizens, active on both Facebook and Twitter with >=50 posts each, and recruited as politically interested (87.2% scored at or above the scale midpoint on political interest), so not a general-population sample. Survey and app-based trace harvest 7 March to 6 June 2017; posts coded 1 August 2015 to 6 June 2017 with users whose account activity began after 1 August 2015 dropped; analytic n = 678 Facebook and 543 Twitter (525 in both). Exposure classification is automated domain matching against a list pooled from eleven published fake-news lists with a two-list threshold, so no human coding and no intercoder reliability; the authors themselves note (Note 7) that such lists have been criticised for including hyper-partisan rather than outright false sites. Missing data judged MCAR by Little's test.
rob.item6_quote: To appear in our list, a site had to appear on at least two of the identified fake news domain lists. In total, we identified 106 countermedia websites.
rob.item10_quote: In the Facebook sample, a total of 1,152 countermedia content shares were identified. The maximum number of pieces of content shared by a single user was 171. The majority of respondents (71.1%) did not share any countermedia items.
